scope: Claim-level reproductive-development, photoperiod, floral morphology, pollen, fertilization, seed maturation, sex-expression, senescence, and reproductive-record evidence for remaining unmapped THC-ENC-201 through THC-ENC-220 lessons.
rules: Photoperiod and developmental timing remain cultivar-, endpoint-, and environment-dependent; no tested schedule is generalized as a universal cannabis constant.
Pollen appearance, staining, germination, transport, deposition, fertilization, and seed formation are distinct biological and measurement stages.
Review and general plant evidence support interpretation but do not replace cannabis-specific experimental evidence where performance thresholds are claimed.
Claim mapping does not constitute independent science review, publication authorization, assessment approval, or visual approval.

claimEvidence.supportedClaim: The cannabis transition toward reproductive development is staged and genotype-dependent: solitary floral development, photoperiod-triggered inflorescence morphogenesis, and cultivar-specific flowering initiation should not be collapsed into one universal calendar event.
claimEvidence.sourceLocator: Ahrens et al. 2023 abstract/results across ten cultivars; Spitzer-Rimon et al. 2019 florogenesis observations; Alter et al. 2024 abstract/results on short-day inflorescence morphogenesis.
claimEvidence.applicability: Supports staged developmental records and separation of preflower, floral initiation, and inflorescence development.
claimEvidence.limitations: Definitions and timing endpoints differ among studies and cultivars; exact day counts are not universal.

claimEvidence.supportedClaim: Cannabis/hemp flowering response varies among cultivars and can shift over photoperiod differences smaller than one hour, so 12/12 is a common production convention rather than a universal biological critical photoperiod.
claimEvidence.sourceLocator: Ahrens et al. 2023 12–15 h indoor photoperiod experiment; Zhang et al. 2021 controlled photoperiod experiments across essential-oil, grain, and fiber hemp cultivars.
claimEvidence.applicability: Supports cultivar-specific photoperiod thresholds and explicit flowering endpoints.
claimEvidence.limitations: Thresholds depend on cultivar, source, environment, light intensity, endpoint, and experiment duration.

claimEvidence.supportedClaim: Solitary cannabis flowers and sex-specific floral structures can appear before full inflorescence development, so visible preflowers indicate reproductive development without proving whole-plant flowering stage or a universal maturity threshold.
claimEvidence.sourceLocator: Spitzer-Rimon et al. 2019 solitary-flower/florogenesis observations; Punja and Holmes 2020 pistillate, staminate, and intersex floral morphology.
claimEvidence.applicability: Supports anatomical confirmation of preflowers and node-position phenology records.
claimEvidence.limitations: Visible timing and node position vary among genotypes and environments; no fixed age or node count is established.

claimEvidence.supportedClaim: Female cannabis inflorescences are structured assemblies of many floral and supporting organs whose architecture varies with developmental position and plant architecture; visual compactness alone does not establish maturity or chemistry.
claimEvidence.sourceLocator: Spitzer-Rimon et al. 2019 architecture/florogenesis; Punja and Holmes 2020 reproductive morphology; Shape Matters 2021 within-plant positional/chemical variation.
claimEvidence.applicability: Supports measurement of inflorescence position, size, density, and associated canopy context.
claimEvidence.limitations: Terminology and morphology vary across genotypes and studies; architecture does not independently determine chemical quality.

claimEvidence.supportedClaim: In the studied female cannabis material, short-day transition produced an initial phase of rapid internode/stem elongation followed by reduced elongation and condensed inflorescence formation, demonstrating that early-flower stretch is a developmental phase rather than a universal multiplier.
claimEvidence.sourceLocator: Alter et al. 2024 abstract and results on the two-phase short-day response.
claimEvidence.applicability: Supports repeated height/internode measurements through reproductive transition.
claimEvidence.limitations: Exact timing and magnitude were observed in a limited cultivar context and should not be generalized.

claimEvidence.supportedClaim: Mature staminate cannabis flowers release pollen, but visible anther maturity, pollen quantity, atmospheric release, and functional pollen viability are separate observations that should be recorded independently.
claimEvidence.sourceLocator: Punja and Holmes 2020 staminate/anther morphology; Gaudet et al. 2020 developmental-stage/germination work; Nimmala et al. 2024 pollen transport context.
claimEvidence.applicability: Supports anthesis staging and separation of pollen release from viability.
claimEvidence.limitations: Diurnal release timing and quantity vary with genotype and environment and are not universally characterized.

claimEvidence.supportedClaim: Cannabis pollen structural/non-abortion measures and in-vitro germination measure different properties and can diverge, so appearance or staining alone cannot substitute for a functional germination assay.
claimEvidence.sourceLocator: Gaudet et al. 2020 germination assay and storage study; Wizenberg et al. 2022 paired non-abortion and germination/viability comparisons.
claimEvidence.applicability: Supports explicit pollen-fitness method naming and separation of morphology from functional viability.
claimEvidence.limitations: In-vitro germination remains a laboratory proxy and does not guarantee successful fertilization in planta.

claimEvidence.supportedClaim: Pollen receipt is not equivalent to completed fertilization: compatible pollen must germinate and grow pollen tubes before fertilization, after which cannabis inflorescence development and chemistry can diverge from unfertilized controls.
claimEvidence.sourceLocator: Punja and Holmes 2020 pollen germination/pollen-tube observations; Lipson Feder et al. 2021 fertilized-versus-unfertilized cannabis inflorescence study.
claimEvidence.applicability: Supports the sequence from pollination to fertilization and early seed-development evidence.
claimEvidence.limitations: Detailed hour-by-hour cannabis embryo development across cultivars remains incompletely characterized.

claimEvidence.supportedClaim: In the tested cannabis chemovars, fertilization after pollination changed subsequent inflorescence development and predominantly reduced phytocannabinoid accumulation while terpenoid responses varied, supporting seedless production as pollen/fertilization exclusion rather than a universal potency rule.
claimEvidence.sourceLocator: Lipson Feder et al. 2021 abstract, results, and conclusions comparing fertilized and unfertilized inflorescences.
claimEvidence.applicability: Supports biological explanation of seedless flower production and the distinction between reproductive state and chemical testing.
claimEvidence.limitations: Magnitude and direction of chemistry changes vary by compound and chemovar; no universal potency-loss percentage is established.

claimEvidence.supportedClaim: Cannabis pollen storage performance depends on developmental stage, preparation, storage conditions, and the viability assay used; a validated cryogenic protocol cannot be generalized to ordinary freezer storage or indefinite shelf life.
claimEvidence.sourceLocator: Gaudet et al. 2020 developmental-stage and cryopreservation/germination results; Wizenberg et al. 2022 room/freezer pollen-fitness comparisons.
claimEvidence.applicability: Supports storage-history records and post-storage functional testing.
claimEvidence.limitations: Published protocols differ and measured proxies are not interchangeable; no universal storage duration is established.

claimEvidence.supportedClaim: Cannabis pollen is mobile in air and can be captured/quantified with defined methods, so containment should be managed as source-pathway-recipient risk with workflow and viability controls rather than a single guaranteed isolation distance or cleanup method.
claimEvidence.sourceLocator: Nimmala et al. 2024 atmospheric dispersal modeling; Wizenberg et al. 2020 controlled capture/quantification methods; Gaudet et al. 2020 viability context.
claimEvidence.applicability: Supports containment, transfer-pathway records, and verification of pollen-control procedures.
claimEvidence.limitations: These sources do not establish one universal room-decontamination protocol or zero-risk isolation radius.

claimEvidence.supportedClaim: Hemp seed maturation can be heterogeneous, and mature, semi-mature, and immature seed groups differ in germination/emergence performance, supporting direct maturity and seed-quality records rather than one visual rule.
claimEvidence.sourceLocator: Yılmaz, Yıldırım, and Gür 2025 germination/emergence comparison across maturity stages.
claimEvidence.applicability: Supports asynchronous seed-maturation and postharvest quality-testing concepts.
claimEvidence.limitations: The study concerns hemp material and does not define a universal harvest percentage, color, or days-after-pollination threshold for all cannabis seed crops.

claimEvidence.supportedClaim: Cannabis sex expression is context-dependent and can reflect interacting genetic, hormonal, developmental, treatment, and environmental factors, so one observed stressor should not be assigned as the sole cause of intersex expression without stronger evidence.
claimEvidence.sourceLocator: Richards et al. 2026 review abstract/synthesis; Alter et al. 2024 reproductive hormone/photoperiod study; Punja and Holmes 2020 intersex floral morphology.
claimEvidence.applicability: Supports repeated phenotyping and environment/treatment records for intersex monitoring.
claimEvidence.limitations: The review summarizes heterogeneous evidence; universal environmental trigger thresholds are not established.

claimEvidence.supportedClaim: In the studied female cannabis material, returning short-day plants to long days increased internode elongation and disrupted condensed inflorescence architecture, demonstrating reversible photoperiod-regulated morphology rather than a simple developmental clock reset.
claimEvidence.sourceLocator: Alter et al. 2024 abstract/results on return-to-long-day treatment and inflorescence disassembly.
claimEvidence.applicability: Supports biological explanation of reversion/revegetative morphology and reflowering as a new transition.
claimEvidence.limitations: Reversion timing, cloning success, and later yield were not established universally across modern cultivars.

claimEvidence.supportedClaim: Cannabis glandular trichome morphology and maturation vary with plant age and genotype and can be asynchronous within inflorescences, so trichome appearance is an informative but imperfect maturity indicator rather than a universal harvest threshold.
claimEvidence.sourceLocator: Livingston et al. 2023 trichome development, morphology, maturation, age, genotype, and postharvest observations.
claimEvidence.applicability: Supports microscopy sampling and caution around color-only harvest rules.
claimEvidence.limitations: Visual trichome state does not independently establish a target cannabinoid profile or optimal harvest time for every genotype.

claimEvidence.supportedClaim: Reproductive records should preserve parent/sample identity, developmental or maturity state, handling/storage history, testing method, and lot relationships because those variables materially affect pollen and seed outcomes and later interpretation.
claimEvidence.sourceLocator: Gaudet et al. 2020 pollen stage/storage/testing metadata; Yılmaz et al. 2025 seed maturity/performance; MIAPPE v1.2 experiment/biological-material/observation metadata structure.
claimEvidence.applicability: Supports traceable parent-to-pollination-to-seed-lot documentation and explicit links to later tests.
claimEvidence.limitations: Records preserve intended and observed identity but do not prove genetic parentage or replace seed-quality/molecular testing.
